# How much did Germany really pay in reparations from the Treaty of Versailles?

Vice President Charles G. Dawes. (3 March 1925). Library of Congress, Item No. 2016850138. Public Domain. Source: https://www.loc.gov/item/2016850138/

 During the 1920s, American banks lent Germany more money than Germany ever paid in reparations for the First World War. 

 The Inter-Allied Reparation Commission had announced a bill of 132 billion gold marks in April 1921, and the figure became one of the most politically explosive numbers of the twentieth century. 

 In practice, 82 billion of that total existed only on paper, and the payments Germany did make between 1920 and 1931, roughly 20 billion gold marks, relied heavily on borrowed American capital. 

 When American lending stopped during the Great Depression, the entire reparations system collapsed with it. 

## What the treaty actually said about reparations

 Since the Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, public discussion of reparations has focused on the enormous sums Germany was supposedly required to pay. 

 Article 231, which is now more commonly known as the “war guilt clause,” declared Germany and its allies responsible for all losses suffered by the Allied nations during the war. 

 Article 232 required Germany to compensate Allied civilian populations for wartime damage. 

 Crucially, the treaty did not specify a total figure. Instead, the Allies established an interim payment of 20 billion gold marks, due by May 1921, and created the Reparation Commission to determine the final amount. 

 The commission took two years to calculate the sum, and the delay gave German politicians time to build domestic opposition to whatever number eventually appeared. 

 By the time the figure was announced at the London Conference in April 1921, the German public was already primed to reject it. 

## The hidden structure behind 132 billion gold marks

 When the commission announced its figure, the headline number was 132 billion gold marks, roughly US$33 billion at the time. 

 Germany was expected to pay annual instalments of 2 billion marks, plus a sum equal to 26 per cent of the value of its annual exports. 

 At first glance, this amount appeared crushing. In practice, though, the obligation was considerably smaller. 

 The 132 billion was divided into three categories of bonds. A bonds accounted for 12 billion marks, and B bonds accounted for another 38 billion marks, meaning these two categories totalled 50 billion marks. 

 The remaining 82 billion consisted of C bonds, which were not scheduled for repayment until Germany had finished paying off the first two categories. 

 Sally Marks described the C bonds as “entirely chimerical,” arguing that they existed primarily as a political device to convince the French and British publics that Germany was being punished severely. 

 For this reason, the true obligation that Germany faced in 1921 was closer to 50 billion gold marks, not the 132 billion that dominated newspaper headlines. 

 Even this reduced figure was substantial, as it was roughly equivalent to Germany’s entire national income for one year. 

 Nonetheless, the gap between the headline number and the actual requirement is significant, because it shows that the Allied governments themselves expected to collect considerably less than the figure they announced publicly. 

## Why Germany stopped paying after only two years

 In May 1921, Germany made its first instalment of 1 billion gold marks in gold and hard currency, with the payment divided between France and Belgium. 

 After that initial transfer, the German government argued that further payments were damaging the economy. 

 By late 1922, Germany had fallen behind on deliveries of coal and timber, which also counted toward the reparations total. 

 In January 1923, the Reparation Commission declared Germany in default. French Prime Minister Raymond Poincaré responded by ordering French and Belgian troops to occupy the Ruhr, Germany’s most productive industrial region. 

 Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno’s government encouraged Ruhr workers to pursue passive resistance and refuse cooperation with the occupying forces. 

 As a result, industrial output in the region collapsed, and the government printed money to support the striking workers. 

 The consequences were catastrophic, since hyperinflation consumed the German economy throughout 1923, and by November of that year, one US dollar was worth 4.2 trillion marks. 

 The Reichsmark had become worthless and savings were destroyed. Ordinary Germans experienced economic devastation on a scale that no European country had known in peacetime.

## How the Dawes and Young plans reduced the bill

 As a result of the crisis, an international committee led by American financier Charles G. Dawes proposed a new payment schedule in 1924. 

 Under the Dawes Plan, Germany would pay 1 billion marks in the first year, with the amount gradually increasing to 2.5 billion marks per year by the fifth year. 

 The plan also reorganised the German central bank and introduced a stable new currency called the Reichsmark. 

 To stabilise the economy, the committee arranged US$200 million in international loans from American banks. 

 For five years, the Dawes Plan appeared to work. American money flowed into Germany, and Germany used a portion of it to make reparation payments to France and Britain, who in turn used those payments to repay their own war debts to the United States. 

 The arrangement depended entirely on continued American lending. 

 By 1929, a new committee chaired by American businessman Owen D. Young proposed another revision. 

 The Young Plan reduced Germany’s total obligation to 112 billion Reichsmarks, payable over 59 years until 1988, and established the Bank for International Settlements to manage the transfer of funds. 

 Annual payments were set at roughly 2 billion marks, with one-third designated as unconditional and the remaining two-thirds eligible for postponement in times of economic difficulty. 

Charles G. Dawes. (19 March 1925). Library of Congress, Item No. 2002697182. Public Domain. Source: https://www.loc.gov/item/2002697182/

## How the Great Depression ended reparations altogether

 Within months of the Young Plan taking effect in September 1930, the global depression had gutted the international economy. 

 American banks stopped lending to Germany, which meant the circular flow of money that had sustained reparation payments dried up almost immediately. 

 In mid-1931, the Danat-Bank, Germany’s second-largest financial institution, collapsed. The country then suspended gold convertibility. 

 In July 1931, US President Herbert Hoover announced a one-year moratorium on all reparation payments and inter-government war debts. 

 Expert commissions concluded that Germany would be unable to resume payments once the moratorium expired. 

 At the Lausanne Conference in June and July 1932, the major Allied creditor nations and Germany agreed to cancel approximately 90 per cent of Germany’s remaining obligations, requesting only a final bond deposit of 3 billion Reichsmarks. 

 That deposit was never paid. Adolf Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor in January 1933 ended any prospect of further reparation payments, because the Nazi government refused to honour any obligations under the Treaty of Versailles. 

## What did Germany actually pay?

 Between 1920 and 1931, Germany transferred approximately 20 billion gold marks in total reparation payments. 

 Of that sum, roughly 12.5 billion was in cash, and the remainder consisted of deliveries in kind, such as coal and chemical products. 

 In dollar terms, the total came to approximately US$5 billion, a small portion of the 132 billion gold marks announced in 1921. 

 Even more significantly, historian Stephen Schuker has argued that Germany received more in American loans during the 1920s than it paid in reparations. 

 Under the Dawes and Young plans, US loans to Germany exceeded US$3 billion, meaning American investors effectively financed the reparation payments. 

 When Germany defaulted on those loans during the Depression, the cost fell on American bondholders, not German taxpayers. 

 The reparations question did not end there, however. In 1953, West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed the London Debt Agreement, which committed the Federal Republic to repaying outstanding bonds from the 1920s. 

 Under the agreement, roughly half of the pre-war debt was cancelled, and repayment of the rest was stretched over decades. 

 West Germany paid off the principal by 1980, but one clause deferred certain interest payments until German reunification. 

 After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and reunification in 1990, the German government resumed those final interest payments. 

 On 3 October 2010, exactly twenty years after reunification, Germany made its last payment of 69.9 million euros, closing the books on the Treaty of Versailles ninety-two years after the end of the war. 

## Did reparations really cripple Germany?

 British economist John Maynard Keynes established the dominant interpretation of reparations in 1920, when his book “The Economic Consequences of the Peace” argued that the Allies had imposed a punitive settlement that would bankrupt Germany. 

 For fifty years, most historians accepted this view. Since the 1970s, scholars including Sally Marks and Marc Trachtenberg have challenged that interpretation, pointing out that the actual burden was considerably lighter than the headline figures suggested. 

 Marks argued that German governments worked deliberately to undermine the reparation system from its earliest years by defaulting strategically and exploiting domestic outrage over the war guilt clause. 

 The true cost of reparations was probably political above all else: the resentment they generated provided fuel for extremist movements, including the Nazi Party, and proved more destructive to European stability than the payments themselves ever could have been.
